analysis.one_liner: Bans rental application and screening fees, caps late fees, and requires renters get upfront cost disclosures.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced June 24, 2025 by Sen. Merkley with one cosponsor and has sat in the Senate Banking Committee with no vote or further action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar owners of federally backed or federally assisted rental units from charging application fees or fees for background and credit checks, cap late fees below 3% of monthly rent and only after rent is 15 days overdue, and require landlords to disclose the true monthly cost, past tenant lawsuits, building maintenance problems, and the property's 10-year rent history before a lease is signed. It would also direct the consumer finance and trade regulators to write rules defining rental "junk fees" and to stop landlords from reporting unpaid junk fees to credit bureaus.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters in units covered by the bill — any rental unit that receives federal housing assistance or sits on a property with an FHA, VA, USDA, Fannie Mae, or Freddie Mac mortgage loan. They save application and screening fees that today are charged before anyone knows whether they'll get the apartment, face smaller and later late fees, and learn the real monthly cost and the building's problems before signing. Renters also gain protection from junk fees being used to damage their credit.

how_it_helps.text: Bans landlords from charging any fee to apply to rent a covered unit, so rejected applicants no longer pay for the privilege of being turned down.
Bans fees for criminal history, tenant screening, consumer report, or other background checks on applicants.
Caps late fees below 3% of monthly rent and prohibits charging any late fee until rent is 15 days past due, with the rules disclosed in the lease.

Requires landlords to disclose before signing: total monthly amount due including fees, a summary of past litigation with tenants, ongoing pest and maintenance issues, and the rent increase in each of the last 10 years.

Directs the CFPB and FTC to write a rule defining rental junk fees and to treat reporting an unpaid junk fee to a credit bureau as an unfair debt collection practice under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act.

Coverage is broad on the rental side: it reaches units receiving federal housing assistance and units on properties with federally backed mortgages, including FHA, VA, USDA, and Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac loans.

analysis.who_pays: Landlords and property owners of covered units lose application and screening fee revenue and face caps on late fees, plus new disclosure duties before each lease. Tenant screening and background-check companies lose a billing channel landlords currently pass through to applicants. Some landlords may try to recover the lost fee income through higher advertised rent.

drawbacks.text: Coverage is tied to federal money: units whose buildings carry no federal housing assistance and no federally backed mortgage are entirely outside the bill, leaving many renters unprotected.
Landlords lose fee income and small landlords in particular lose the ability to charge any late fee for two weeks after rent is due, a real cash-flow cost for owners living on rental income.

Most provisions are mandates on regulators rather than self-executing rules — the fee bans and disclosure rules take effect through later rulemaking by HUD, the VA, USDA, the housing finance regulator, and the CFPB/FTC — so benefits depend on agencies actually writing and enforcing those rules.
Landlord groups would argue that banned fees and disclosure duties raise compliance costs that get folded into rent, partially offsetting renter savings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For renters in covered units, the gains are concrete and immediate: fees charged just to apply, fees for background checks, and inflated late fees go to zero or shrink, and disclosure of total monthly cost and building problems prevents move-in surprises. The costs fall on landlords and screening companies, and some portion may resurface in advertised rent, but fee-shifting to upfront prices is exactly what lets renters comparison shop. The main weakness is design, not cost: the bill only reaches federally financed units, so a large share of the rental market gets no protection at all.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee in June 2025, and nothing has happened to it since — no hearing, no vote, and no floor action.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the End Junk Fees for Renters Act on June 24, 2025, joined in the introduction by Sen. Bernie Sanders.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day, which is where the record ends.
The bill has one cosponsor in addition to the lead sponsor, and the committee has taken no recorded action on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, landlords, property managers, and tenant screening companies are better off: because the bill has not advanced, the application fees, screening fees, and uncapped late fees it targets remain fully in place. Renters have gained nothing yet, but the Congress is still in session so the bill is not dead.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Landlords and screening companies, so far

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Banking Committee

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its only cosponsor

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred and no opposition has appeared on the record; the bill's two sponsors are a Democrat and an Independent, with no Republican cosponsors so far.

industries.note: The bill eliminates application and screening fees that landlords currently collect from applicants, caps late fees at under 3% of rent and 15 days out, and imposes pre-lease disclosure duties. For covered units, junk fee revenue ends and pricing becomes more transparent.

industries.industry: Tenant screening and background check companies
industries.note: Landlords currently pass the cost of screening reports to applicants; the bill bans passing those costs to applicants, and the CFPB/FTC rule would bar reporting unpaid junk fees to credit bureaus, shrinking the industry's leverage over renters.

The bill would classify reporting unpaid rental junk fees to credit bureaus as an unfair debt collection practice, cutting off one stream of collection-related data, though routine rent reporting is untouched.

analysis.trajectory: With a single cosponsor and no committee action five months after introduction, the bill is likely to sit in the Banking Committee without a hearing or vote unless it is folded into a larger housing package; most single-sponsor housing bills in a divided Senate never reach the floor.
